modules.title: 6.1 Water: Structure, Properties and Purification
modules.html:
Water is the most abundant compound on earth (about 71% of the surface) and the medium in which nearly all biological chemistry happens. Its molecule is bent, with a bond angle of about 104.5°, because the oxygen atom carries two lone pairs that repel the bonding pairs more strongly than the bonding pairs repel one another.

Oxygen is far more electronegative than hydrogen, so each O–H bond is polar; because the molecule is bent the dipoles do not cancel and the molecule as a whole is polar. This polarity, together with hydrogen bonding, explains almost every unusual property of water:

  • Abnormally high boiling point (100°C) compared with \(H_2S\) (−60°C): hydrogen bonds must be broken before molecules escape.
  • High specific heat capacity (4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) — moderates climate and makes water a good coolant in radiators.
  • High latent heat of vaporisation (2.26 MJ kg⁻¹) — sweating cools the body efficiently.
  • Maximum density at 4°C — ice floats, so ponds freeze from the top and aquatic life survives beneath.
  • Excellent solvent for ionic and polar substances — hence called the "universal solvent".

Chemical behaviour

  • With very reactive metals: \(2Na + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + H_2\)
  • With moderately reactive metals (steam): \(3Fe + 4H_2O \rightleftharpoons Fe_3O_4 + 4H_2\)
  • With acidic oxides: \(SO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2SO_3\); with basic oxides: \(CaO + H_2O \rightarrow Ca(OH)_2\)
  • Hydrolysis: \(PCl_3 + 3H_2O \rightarrow H_3PO_3 + 3HCl\)
  • Hydration (reversible, no new substance): \(CuSO_4 + 5H_2O \rightleftharpoons CuSO_4\!\cdot\!5H_2O\)

Tests for water

Physical: colourless liquid boiling at 100°C and freezing at 0°C at 1 atm. Chemical: turns white anhydrous \(CuSO_4\) blue, or blue anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride pink. Note that these tests show water is present; only the boiling/freezing points prove it is pure.

Municipal water treatment

  1. Screening — bars remove leaves, sticks, refuse.
  2. Sedimentation — heavy solids settle in large tanks.
  3. Coagulation/flocculation — alum, \(KAl(SO_4)_2\), forms a gelatinous \(Al(OH)_3\) floc that traps fine clay particles.
  4. Filtration — beds of sand and gravel remove remaining suspended matter and many bacteria.
  5. Chlorination — chlorine or sodium hypochlorite kills pathogens; \(Cl_2+H_2O\rightarrow HCl+HOCl\), and HOCl is the germicide.
  6. Fluoridation and pH correction — small amounts of fluoride protect teeth; lime adjusts pH before distribution.

Laboratory-pure water is obtained by distillation or by ion exchange; distilled water is used in car batteries and in preparing standard solutions because tap water contains dissolved ions.

examples.q: Why does ice float on water, and why does this matter ecologically?
examples.a: Below 4°C hydrogen bonds force molecules into an open hexagonal lattice, so ice is less dense than liquid water. Ice therefore forms an insulating layer on the surface, allowing fish and plants to survive in the liquid water below.

examples.q: State one chemical and one physical test for water.
examples.a: Chemical: it turns white anhydrous copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) blue. Physical: a pure sample boils at exactly 100°C and freezes at 0°C at standard pressure.

examples.q: Why is alum added during water treatment?
examples.a: It hydrolyses to give a gelatinous aluminium hydroxide floc which adsorbs and drags down fine suspended clay and colloidal particles that will not settle on their own.

modules.title: 6.2 Hardness of Water and Its Removal
modules.html:
Hard water is water that does not readily form lather with soap; instead it produces an insoluble grey scum. Hardness is caused by dissolved \(Ca^{2+}\) and \(Mg^{2+}\) ions, which react with the sodium stearate/palmitate in soap:

$$2C_{17}H_{35}COONa + Ca^{2+} \rightarrow (C_{17}H_{35}COO)_2Ca\downarrow + 2Na^+$$

Types of hardness

Temporary hardnessPermanent hardness
Causehydrogentrioxocarbonates(IV): \(Ca(HCO_3)_2\), \(Mg(HCO_3)_2\)sulphates and chlorides: \(CaSO_4\), \(MgSO_4\), \(CaCl_2\)
How it formsrain water + \(CO_2\) dissolves limestone: \(CaCO_3+H_2O+CO_2\rightarrow Ca(HCO_3)_2\)water percolates through gypsum or magnesium salt deposits
Removed by boiling?YesNo

Methods of softening

  • Boiling (temporary only): \(Ca(HCO_3)_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} CaCO_3\downarrow + H_2O + CO_2\). The precipitated carbonate is the "fur" or scale in kettles and boilers.
  • Addition of slaked lime (Clark's process, temporary only): \(Ca(HCO_3)_2 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow 2CaCO_3\downarrow + 2H_2O\). Excess lime must be avoided or it makes the water hard again.
  • Washing soda (both types): \(CaSO_4 + Na_2CO_3 \rightarrow CaCO_3\downarrow + Na_2SO_4\).
  • Ion exchange (both types) — the modern industrial method. Water passes through a resin (permutit, a sodium aluminosilicate) which swaps its \(Na^+\) for \(Ca^{2+}/Mg^{2+}\). The exhausted resin is regenerated with concentrated brine. A cation + anion resin bed together gives fully deionised water.
  • Distillation (both types) — effective but expensive on a large scale.
  • Complexing agents — sodium hexametaphosphate (Calgon) and EDTA lock up the metal ions in soluble complexes.

Advantages and disadvantages of hard water

Advantages: supplies calcium for bones and teeth; pleasant taste; \(CaSO_4\) coating protects lead pipes from poisoning the supply; valuable in brewing and tanning.

Disadvantages: wastes soap; leaves scum on clothes and baths; furs kettles and blocks boiler tubes, wasting fuel and risking explosion; spoils some dyeing and laundry processes.

Detergents (soapless) do not form scum because their calcium and magnesium salts are soluble — but many are non-biodegradable and cause foaming and eutrophication in rivers.

examples.q: A sample of water lathers only after boiling. What kind of hardness does it contain, and which ions are responsible?
examples.a: Temporary hardness, caused by calcium and magnesium hydrogentrioxocarbonates(IV). Boiling decomposes them to insoluble carbonates, so the Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ are removed.

examples.q: Write an equation for the removal of permanent hardness with washing soda.
examples.a: \(MgSO_4+Na_2CO_3\rightarrow MgCO_3\downarrow+Na_2SO_4\). The offending Mg²⁺ is precipitated as insoluble carbonate.

examples.q: Explain how the permutit process softens water and how the resin is regenerated.
examples.a: Water flows over a sodium aluminosilicate resin; Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ in the water exchange with Na⁺ on the resin, so only harmless sodium ions remain in solution. When the resin is saturated it is flushed with concentrated NaCl solution, which reverses the exchange and restores the sodium form.

modules.title: 6.3 Solutions, Solubility and Solubility Curves
modules.html:
A solution is a homogeneous mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent. Three states are recognised at a given temperature:

  • Unsaturated — can still dissolve more solute.
  • Saturated — contains all the solute it can dissolve in the presence of undissolved solute, i.e. an equilibrium exists between dissolved and undissolved solute.
  • Supersaturated — contains more solute than a saturated solution at that temperature; unstable, and crystallises suddenly when seeded or scratched. Made by cooling a hot saturated solution slowly and without disturbance.

Defining solubility

The solubility of a solute is the maximum amount (in moles or grams) that saturates 1 dm³ (or 100 g) of solvent at a stated temperature.

$$S\ (mol\,dm^{-3}) = \frac{\text{mass of solute that saturates } 1\,dm^3}{\text{molar mass}}$$

A common experimental route: evaporate a known volume of saturated solution to dryness, weigh the residue, and scale up.

$$\text{Solubility per 100 g water} = \frac{\text{mass of solute}}{\text{mass of water}}\times100$$

Factors affecting solubility

  • Temperature — for most solids solubility rises with temperature (\(KNO_3\) sharply, NaCl only slightly). For \(Ca(OH)_2\) and \(Na_2SO_4\) above 32.4°C it falls. For gases solubility always falls as temperature rises — which is why warm rivers hold less dissolved oxygen (thermal pollution).
  • Pressure — no significant effect on solids and liquids; for gases, solubility is proportional to pressure (Henry's law) — hence the fizz when a bottle of soft drink is opened.
  • Nature of solute and solvent — "like dissolves like": ionic and polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents (water); non-polar solutes (fats, iodine, sulphur) dissolve in non-polar solvents (benzene, \(CCl_4\), petrol).

Solubility curves

A graph of solubility (y-axis) against temperature (x-axis). Uses:

  1. Read off the solubility at any temperature, or the temperature at which a given solubility occurs.
  2. Calculate the mass of crystals deposited when a saturated solution is cooled: mass = (solubility at higher T − solubility at lower T) × mass of water/100.
  3. Compare solutes and choose conditions for fractional crystallisation — separating two salts whose solubility curves diverge sharply, e.g. \(KNO_3\) from NaCl.
  4. Detect changes of hydration: a sharp break in the curve (e.g. \(Na_2SO_4\) at 32.4°C) shows a change from decahydrate to anhydrous form.

Precipitation and solubility product

For a sparingly soluble salt \(A_xB_y\), the equilibrium \(A_xB_y \rightleftharpoons xA^{y+} + yB^{x-}\) gives

$$K_{sp} = [A^{y+}]^x[B^{x-}]^y$$

Precipitation occurs when the ionic product exceeds \(K_{sp}\). Adding an ion already present (the common ion effect) lowers solubility — for instance, AgCl is even less soluble in dilute NaCl solution than in pure water.

examples.q: 50 g of water at 60°C dissolved 55 g of \(KNO_3\) to saturation. Calculate the solubility in g per 100 g of water.
examples.a: Solubility = (55/50) × 100 = 110 g per 100 g of water at 60°C.

examples.q: The solubility of a salt is 40 g/100 g water at 70°C and 15 g/100 g water at 20°C. What mass crystallises when 200 g of water saturated at 70°C is cooled to 20°C?
examples.a: Difference = 40 − 15 = 25 g per 100 g water. For 200 g water: 25 × 2 = 50 g of crystals deposited.

examples.q: Why does a warm bottle of soft drink fizz more violently than a cold one?
examples.a: Gas solubility falls as temperature rises, so warm liquid holds less dissolved CO₂ and the excess escapes rapidly when the pressure is released.

modules.title: 6.4 Concentration, Standard Solutions and Colloids
modules.html:
Expressing concentration

  • Mass concentration (g dm⁻³) = mass of solute / volume of solution in dm³.
  • Molar concentration (mol dm⁻³, "molarity"): $$C = \frac{n}{V} = \frac{m}{M \times V}$$
  • Conversion: concentration in g dm⁻³ = molarity × molar mass.
  • Percentage by mass = (mass of solute / mass of solution) × 100.
  • Parts per million (ppm) = mg of solute per dm³ of solution — used for trace pollutants and for water hardness.

Dilution

Adding solvent changes the volume but not the number of moles of solute, so

$$C_1V_1 = C_2V_2$$

To make 250 cm³ of 0.1 M HCl from 1.0 M stock: \(V_1 = (0.1\times250)/1.0 = 25\ cm^3\), then make up to the mark with distilled water in a volumetric flask.

Preparing a standard solution

  1. Weigh the calculated mass of primary standard accurately on a chemical balance.
  2. Dissolve in a small volume of distilled water in a beaker; stir until fully dissolved.
  3. Transfer to a volumetric flask, rinsing the beaker and funnel into the flask so no solute is lost.
  4. Add water to just below the graduation mark, then dropwise until the bottom of the meniscus sits on the mark at eye level.
  5. Stopper and invert repeatedly to mix thoroughly.

Types of mixtures by particle size

SolutionColloidSuspension
Particle size< 1 nm1–1000 nm> 1000 nm
Appearanceclearoften cloudycloudy, settles
Filterable?nono (ordinary filter)yes
Tyndall effectnoyesyes
Examplessalt watermilk, fog, paint, gelmuddy water, chalk in water

The Tyndall effect is the scattering of a light beam by colloidal particles — it makes a torch beam visible in fog or in a glass of dilute milk, and is the simplest way to distinguish a colloid from a true solution.

Emulsions and emulsifiers

An emulsion is a colloid of one liquid dispersed in another (oil in water in milk and mayonnaise). An emulsifier such as soap, detergent or lecithin has a hydrophilic head and a hydrophobic tail; it sits at the oil–water interface and stops the droplets coalescing. This is exactly how soap removes grease during washing.

examples.q: Calculate the mass of \(Na_2CO_3\) needed to prepare 250 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ solution. (Na=23, C=12, O=16)
What volume of 2.0 M HCl is needed to make 500 cm³ of 0.25 M HCl?
examples.a: \(C_1V_1=C_2V_2\): \(V_1=(0.25\times500)/2.0=62.5\ cm^3\). Add acid to water and make up to 500 cm³.

examples.q: How would you show that a sample of milk is a colloid and not a true solution?
examples.a: Shine a narrow beam of light through it. Milk scatters the beam so its path is visible (Tyndall effect); a true solution such as salt water shows no visible beam.
